summary: A landing delay at the Moon’s south pole can improve sunlight and take Earth out of view. AstroSpace’s Lunar Landing Site Navigator compares two landing plans, shows when the Sun and Earth clear the local terrain, and searches for dates that meet user-defined first-week limits. At Connecting Ridge, a 72-hour delay added 48.4 hours of modeled sunlight and reduced Earth visibility from 59.3 hours to zero. A search across 17 sampled landing positions and two terrain models found September 13, 2027 as the first qualifying date with the solar panel and antenna both 5 m above the surface.
details:
What it does: The navigator helps mission planners screen hypothetical landing dates and gives educators and the public a way to explore why terrain matters. Users choose two sites or dates, compare sunlight and Earth-center visibility over the same elapsed time after landing, and move a shared cursor to inspect each local skyline. They can set a minimum continuous overlap and maximum gaps in usable Sun and Earth view, search nearby dates, and share the exact settings or export the UTC windows as CSV.

What the demo shows: At the Connecting Ridge reference point, modeled first-week overlap fell from 10.9 hours to zero when the landing moved from August 27 to August 30, 2027 at the same UTC time. The delayed landing failed the example limits for continuous overlap and time without Earth in view. A daily search beginning on August 30 found September 13 at 00:00 UTC as the first later option at the reference point, with 113.8 hours of continuous overlap at the default 2 m observer height.

Why the touchdown location matters: For Connecting Ridge, users can set the solar panel and antenna heights separately and check a candidate date at 17 sampled positions within 100 m of the reference point. The footprint search applies the same limits to two terrain surfaces. With both heights at 5 m, September 12 passed at all 17 positions on LOLA but at only 15 on the surface refined with LROC images. September 13 was the first date to pass at all 17 positions on both surfaces. Its tightest margin was two hours against the 72-hour limit without usable Sun. With both heights at 2 m, none of the 29 candidate dates passed at all sampled points on both surfaces.

Validation and scope: Across 36 Sun and Earth positions checked against NASA/JPL Horizons, the largest angular separation was 0.005923°. Terrain resolution and time sampling affect the predicted windows. The app screens geometric visibility using the centers of the Sun and Earth. Electrical power and scheduled radio contact require additional mission data, including eclipse timing, panel orientation, antenna specifications, and a link budget.

Development timeline: A working prototype predates the event. During the New York event on November 14, the team refined and tested the footprint search, made comparison links accessible when clipboard access is blocked, documented simulated first-use sessions, and updated the captioned walkthrough.
